heckle

HEK-uhl · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To heckle is to interrupt a speaker or performer with mocking or critical comments.

The comedian handled the hecklers in the front row with practiced ease.

Worked Example

A few fans in the crowd heckled the visiting pitcher every time he stepped up to throw.

Shouting mocking comments specifically at a performer or speaker, again and again, is exactly what heckle describes.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

taunt: To taunt is to fling mocking words at one particular person, trying to sting them into reacting, and it can happen anywhere -- a hallway, a game, a bus line. To heckle is narrower: it means interrupting a speaker or performer mid-act with mocking comments.

boo: To boo is to voice disapproval with a wordless sound -- one long, low note a whole crowd can make at once. To heckle, you need actual words: a heckler breaks into the performance with mocking comments aimed at whoever holds the stage.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

cheer: shout in approval or encouragement

applaud: express approval by clapping

Where it sits · how hostile the disruption becomes — interrupt → heckle → jeer

interrupt vs. heckle: To interrupt is neutral; to heckle is to interrupt specifically with mocking or critical comments.

jeer vs. heckle: To jeer is harsher and more openly hostile than to heckle -- open scorn shouted at any target, a losing team, a rival crowd -- while to heckle is to keep breaking into one speaker's act with mocking comments.

Build the Word

The pieces

Put it together

Put it together: Heckle comes from an old word for a spiked comb used to separate flax fibers -- heckling someone is figuratively 'combing them over' roughly, in front of a crowd.

Use the root in a new word: hackle

Use the root in a new word: hackle: The related word hackle (as in 'raising your hackles') comes from the very same Old English root for a comb-like spike.
